newsitem.title: USA: White House to cease employing DNC-funded staffers.
newsitem.headline: White House to cease employing DNC-funded staffers.

text.p: The White House abruptly announced on Thursday it had decided to end a practice under which it currently employs five people whose salaries are paid by the Democratic National Committee (DNC).

White House spokesman Mike McCurry announced the decision after NBC News reported on Wednesday that one staffer whose salary is financed by the Democratic party had access to a White House database that cannot be used for political work.

"On balance, we'd rather have the four individuals currently on the DNC payroll on the White House payroll and discontinue the practice," McCurry told reporters in a hastily called briefing on Thursday evening.

White House spokesman Barry Toiv later told reporters the White House had concluded that it has five such employees, citing the fifth as a person who does part-time advance work for Vice President Al Gore.
McCurry appeared to suggest that the decision by White House chief of staff Erskine Bowles was prompted in part by the blizzard of media inquiries about the practice.
"Frankly, it's not worth the hassle," McCurry said when asked why the decision had been taken.

Pressed on the matter, he said: "One, it's easier to supervise employees when they are on the White House payroll. Two, frankly we've got plenty of questions that we're dealing with day in and day out (and) we just don't need this set of questions at this time. We'd rather dispense with it."
White House officials said the employees would be moved to the White House payroll "over time," without elaborating.
Earlier on Thursday, the White House said it had employed about 20 such people at various times since 1993.

McCurry, speaking in his midday briefing, said that the arrangement of having the DNC pay for certain workers had been developed to help meet President Bill Clinton's 1992 campaign pledge to cut the White House staff by 25 percent.
"I think it's safe to say that these employment arrangements were made in the context of trying to meet the 25 percent staff cut ordered by the president," he said.

Of the five now at the White House, three work in Gore's office, one in the Office of Public Liaison and one on the scheduling and advance staff. Toiv said their salaries range from $35,000 to $55,000.
McCurry stressed that the White House believes the practice to be legal, saying former President Ronald Reagan had twice sought an opinion from the Justice Department.

The White House made available the second opinion, dated March 27, 1987, in which the Justice Department said it had concluded that there was no reason why someone whose salary was paid by a national political organization "should necessarily be precluded" from working at the White House.

Boyden Gray, former President George Bush's White House Counsel, said the Bush administration had some people whose salaries were paid for by non-governmental groups, but said he did not think there was anyone from the Republican party.
"I am reasonably sure that we had no one from the RNC (Republican National Committee) or from the campaign," adding he did not think there were any during Reagan's two terms.

"It creates too many potential problems -- conflicts of interest, White House confidentiality," he said. "It's just a whole host of problems that could be avoided theoretically but would be very difficult in practice to monitor."
At midday, McCurry said the person named in the NBC News report, Barbara Woolley, had little access to the White House database and had not shared the information outside the White House.

Disclosure of the salary arrangement prompted Republican Rep. David McIntosh of Indiana, who is investigating possible political use of a taxpayer-financed White House database, to demand detailed information on Woolley from the White House.
